doc.title: Jerry Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe and Christian Goodwillie, via Zoom, June 30, 2021

title: First hearing Sun Ra and the Gino's Empty Foxhole concert
summary: Gordon first heard 'Nothing Is' in college and later saw the greatest concert of his life with light show and cloaks at a Penn campus church.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience

blocks.x: You had said in an earlier interview that Sun Ra was always pushing forward, his whole thing was to turn on the light upstairs with as many people as he could come in contact with. So I’m wondering if he turned on any lights for you? Either at this time or later with Evidence?

He turned lights on before I ever met him. When I was in college I had taken a trip to a college in another city to — and I met someone who played for me the album by Sun Ra “Nothing Is.” Okay? And that was my first exposure to Sun Ra, in a dorm room with someone playing the album “Nothing Is.” And it blew my mind. The first listen it blew

my mind. The poetry on the cover, the poetry on the back cover, I mean that — I can’t say it resonated with me I would have to say it blew my mind, the music and the whole presentation. And then it just so happens that when I returned to Philadelphia, you know Sun Ra was living there and I would have opportunities to see him. Crazy. And I saw him which remains to this day the — probably the greatest concert of my life. And it still today binds a lot of people, this concert and this scene. There was a place on University of Pennsylvania campus, St. Mary’s Church, and they allowed this guy to operate a jazz room — you can’t call it a club, there was no alcohol — it was just a space. And it was called Gino’s Empty Foxhole after the guy who was putting together the shows, Gino. And after the Ornette Coleman album title “The Empty Foxhole.” So he was presenting Sun Ra and I went to see him there and it was the greatest show of my life. The light show was incredible and they had fans on the floor blowing air around the room, not to cool off the people in attendance, but Sun Ra and June Tyson had these cloaks. And when you focused the light show on their cloaks and when the fans on the floor blew their cloaks up into the air, Sun Ra and June Tyson were, there was all these colors swirling on their wings, no longer clothes. On their wings. And they were flying around. They were flying. And when I tell this story to people they say well what substance were you on, you know they do that thing. But Sun Ra knew exactly what he was doing. He somehow, I guess he coordinated it with the people operating the light show, I’m not sure. But it was stunning. And I remember them focusing the light show, it was a tunnel-like spiral focused on John Gilmore, the tenor player. And you could almost see notes flying out of his saxophone into the tunnel. It was that great. Another effect I saw that night was they put like this purple — a purple light. And it was on Sun Ra and his cloak. And somehow I don’t even know how he did it, he put the cloak on his head, on his head, really, truthfully, he put it on his head and it gave the appearance that he was sticking his head through a black hole. Because there was Sun Ra without a head. Okay? Just a body. And I wasn’t the only one, everybody at this show was in this trance. It was just stunning. So yeah, getting to see Sun Ra in Philadelphia, which you know I had that opportunity many times, that was, that was the greatest.
